level: serious amateur aiming at professional competence

schools.name: Custodial school
schools.optimises_for: physical custody of records as the basis of archival authority — one archive per record, controlled environment, an unbroken chain of custody
schools.gives_up: speed and scale — born-digital custody at volume is impractical, and distributed stewardship escapes its control model

schools.name: Postcustodial school
schools.optimises_for: describing and preserving records where they are created, especially digital — remote stewardship, distributed custody, intervention at the point of creation
schools.gives_up: the guarantees of controlled physical custody — a single climate, a single chain of custody, one authoritative copy

schools.name: Access-first school
schools.optimises_for: use — reference service, digitization for access, user-centered finding aids, outreach that turns holdings into audiences
schools.gives_up: stewardship depth — less investment in the description and preservation that happen beneath the surface of discovery

schools.name: Preservation-first school
schools.optimises_for: longevity of the physical and digital record — environmental control, conservation, fixity — on the argument that an inaccessible record still exists, a lost one doesn't
schools.gives_up: broad access — throughput, digitization for use, and discovery come second to keeping the thing alive

schools.name: Community archives school
schools.optimises_for: records of and by marginalized communities — participatory control, community ownership of description and access, social justice mandates
schools.gives_up: institutional neutrality — the archive openly takes sides with its community and rejects custody claims over other people's records

clusters.name: Records & archival theory
clusters.gist: What a record is, why provenance and original order bind groups of records together, and the historical arc of the archival function — the vocabulary every later cluster argues in.

clusters.name: Appraisal & acquisition
clusters.gist: Deciding enduring value — Schellenberg's criteria, Terry Cook's macro-appraisal, retention schedules, disposition, and the accessioning that makes a decision legally real.

clusters.name: Arrangement & processing
clusters.gist: Record groups, series, and subseries; respecting original order while making material usable; MPLP's minimal-processing default for backlogs that would otherwise take decades.

clusters.name: Description & finding aids
clusters.gist: Turning arrangement into finding aids and metadata — DACS, EAD, MARC-21, authority control — so a researcher can find and navigate the collection without staff help.

clusters.name: Preservation & conservation
clusters.gist: Keeping the record alive: environmental control, safe handling, reformatting and digitization, disaster response, and digital preservation with fixity and format monitoring.

clusters.name: Access & reference
clusters.gist: Serving the record to people — reading rooms, reference interviews, restrictions, privacy, copyright, outreach — and the policies that decide who sees what, when.

clusters.name: Records management & born-digital
clusters.gist: The front end of the lifecycle: active records, retention schedule authoring, ERM, email and database archives, and transferring born-digital material into the archive intact.

nodes.label: What is a record
nodes.one_line: Distinguish a record from a document or stray information artifact by its provenance and purpose, so you can scope what an archive keeps and defend that scope.

nodes.label: The archival function
nodes.one_line: Place any archives task — appraisal, arrangement, description, preservation, access — on the archival workflow and say which function it serves and what it feeds.

nodes.label: History of archival theory
nodes.one_line: Sketch the theory's arc — Jenkinson's passive custody, Schellenberg's active appraisal, Terry Cook's postcustodial turn — so current debates have named ancestors.

nodes.label: Archives vs. libraries vs. museums
nodes.one_line: Sort archives, libraries, museums, and records centers by mandate and material, so you apply the right professional rules in the right building.

nodes.label: Provenance
nodes.one_line: Trace any body of records to the office or person that created it and use that creator link to explain why the records belong together as one group.

nodes.label: Records lifecycle & continuum
nodes.one_line: Track one record through creation, active use, retention, and disposition on the lifecycle or continuum model, naming where each archival intervention happens.

nodes.label: Archival ethics
nodes.one_line: Apply the SAA Code of Ethics to a donor-restriction or privacy dilemma and write a reasoned call instead of an instinctive one.

nodes.label: Original order
nodes.one_line: Reconstruct the order a creator kept records in — from folder labels, dates, and numbering — so arrangement reflects function instead of your own subject logic.

nodes.label: Reading retention schedules
nodes.one_line: Read an office's retention schedule and sort a mixed batch into permanent, temporary, or destroy, citing the schedule line that justifies each call.

nodes.label: Disposition
nodes.one_line: Execute approved disposition — archive transfer, certified destruction, or hold — so records leave the office legally instead of by accident.

nodes.label: Appraisal criteria
nodes.one_line: Judge a body of records' enduring value with Schellenberg's evidential and informational tests, and state the keep-or-discard call in one paragraph.

nodes.label: Accessioning
nodes.one_line: Process an accession — verify the deed of gift, inventory what physically arrived, assign the accession number — so the archive has legal and physical control from day one.

nodes.label: Macro-appraisal
nodes.one_line: Run Terry Cook's macro-appraisal — evaluate the creating function and its documentation, not individual records — to appraise a whole agency's output at once.

nodes.label: Appraisal report
nodes.one_line: Write an appraisal report that records criteria, evidence, and the disposition recommendation, so the decision survives review years later.

nodes.label: Sampling large series
nodes.one_line: Sample a large homogeneous series — case files, forms — with a statistical or purposive scheme, keeping representative evidence without keeping everything.

nodes.label: Reappraisal & deaccessioning
nodes.one_line: Reappraise an existing holding against current criteria and draft deaccession recommendations with the evidence trail an institution can act on.

nodes.label: Series identification
nodes.one_line: Identify the series inside a body of records by shared function and form, so folders group the way the creator grouped them.

nodes.label: Arrangement plan
nodes.one_line: Plan an accession's arrangement — record groups, series, subseries mirroring creator functions — on paper before touching a single folder.

nodes.label: Physical arrangement
nodes.one_line: Physically order folders into series and subseries on the shelf per the arrangement plan, so the collection reads as the creator's own system.

nodes.label: Rehousing
nodes.one_line: Rehouse material in acid-free folders and boxes sized to the material, so the container stops doing damage the environment would otherwise do.

nodes.label: MPLP minimal processing
nodes.one_line: Apply Greene & Meissner's More Product Less Process — default to minimal processing, keep original order, skip item-level detail — and cut a backlog's processing time from years to months.

nodes.label: Container listing
nodes.one_line: Produce a container list — box and folder numbers with brief contents — that can feed a finding aid without re-opening the boxes.

nodes.label: Item-level arrangement
nodes.one_line: Arrange an item-level collection — photographs, correspondence — where order and provenance live per item, documenting every order decision.

nodes.label: DACS content standard
nodes.one_line: Apply Describing Archives: A Content Standard — required and optional elements, levels of description, grammar rules — to a description you write.

nodes.label: Finding aid
nodes.one_line: Write a DACS-compliant finding aid — collection-level and series-level descriptions, biographical note, scope and content — a researcher can use without staff help.

nodes.label: Authority control
nodes.one_line: Create and reconcile name and subject authority records against VIAF and LCNAF so one creator is spelled and linked identically across every finding aid.

nodes.label: EAD encoding
nodes.one_line: Encode a finding aid in EAD XML that validates against the EAD3 schema and renders in a discovery portal.

nodes.label: MARC-21 catalog records
nodes.one_line: Convert a collection description into MARC-21 records that load into OCLC, so archives holdings surface in library catalogs.

nodes.label: Subject & genre indexing
nodes.one_line: Index a collection with LCSH and form/genre terms, describing what the records are rather than what they mean.

nodes.label: Metadata standards selection
nodes.one_line: Choose a metadata standard per object type — Dublin Core for digital objects, PREMIS for preservation, EAD for finding aids — and justify the choice.

nodes.label: Environmental control
nodes.one_line: Specify the archival storage environment — 65°F ±2, 35-45% relative humidity, under 500 lux with no UV — and verify it with a datalogger.

nodes.label: Handling & storage
nodes.one_line: Handle and store records safely — nitrile gloves for photographs, supports for bound volumes, upright or flat boxing — so use and storage don't damage them.

nodes.label: Disaster response
nodes.one_line: Run the first 48 hours of a disaster — salvage priorities, freezing wet records, freeze-drying referral — so the collection's loss stays partial.

nodes.label: Reformatting options
nodes.one_line: Choose the reformatting that fits the material — microfilm vs digitization, surrogate vs original — weighing use, condition, and cost.

nodes.label: Conservation triage
nodes.one_line: Triage an item's condition — tear, mold, brittle paper — into stabilize-now or refer-to-conservator, documenting exactly what you did and didn't do.

nodes.label: Digitization for access
nodes.one_line: Run a digitization project end to end — scan at 300-600 dpi TIFF with a target, name files per scheme, link surrogates to descriptions — so users get images, not the originals.

nodes.label: Digital preservation
nodes.one_line: Run a digital preservation program — checksum fixity checks, format monitoring, PREMIS/OAIS metadata — so files survive media and format obsolescence.

nodes.label: Format migration
nodes.one_line: Plan a format migration — legacy formats to PDF/A, validating content before and after — so obsolescence doesn't equal loss.

nodes.label: Reading room service
nodes.one_line: Run a reading-room shift — register researchers, enforce the rules, track retrievals — so material is used without being lost, damaged, or stolen.

nodes.label: Reference interview
nodes.one_line: Conduct a reference interview — open question, restated need, material proposed — so you find what the researcher actually needs, not just what they first asked for.

nodes.label: Outreach
nodes.one_line: Plan an outreach program — exhibition, social posts, workshop — with a measurable engagement goal, converting holdings into an audience.

nodes.label: Copyright determinations
nodes.one_line: Make a defensible copyright call for copying or publishing archival material — unpublished status, duration, fair use — and record the reasoning.

nodes.label: User studies
nodes.one_line: Run a small user study — log reference questions, track finding-aid success — and turn the findings into one description or access change.

nodes.label: Restrictions & privacy
nodes.one_line: Apply access restrictions — donor-imposed, statutory, privacy-based — to a request and cite the authority for denying or redacting, documenting the review.

nodes.label: Reference services
nodes.one_line: Run a reference service — interview, retrieval via finding aids, service to in-person and remote users — with policies and statistics, not just ad hoc answers.

nodes.label: Active records systems
nodes.one_line: Set up an office file plan — series folders, naming conventions, version control — so current records are findable without IT archaeology.

nodes.label: Records inventories
nodes.one_line: Run a records inventory — walk the office, list every series with volume and format — producing the data a retention schedule is built from.

nodes.label: Retention schedule authoring
nodes.one_line: Write a retention schedule for an office — every series, retention period, legal hold — so destruction is authorized and auditable, not accidental.

nodes.label: Electronic records management
nodes.one_line: Tame a shared drive or ERM system — classification scheme, capture rules, disposal triggers — so digital records are managed in place instead of accumulating forever.

nodes.label: Email archiving
nodes.one_line: Set up email capture — journaling, retention categories, export to the archive — so institutional memory survives staff departures.

nodes.label: Database archiving
nodes.one_line: Plan the archive of a database — export to CSV or SIARD, document schema and context — so structured data outlives its system.

nodes.label: Born-digital transfer
nodes.one_line: Transfer born-digital records into the archive — write-blocked copies, checksums, technical environment documented — so digital acquisitions arrive intact and provable.
